content.intro: PHP source is parsed and executed by the PHP runtime. Tags mark PHP regions, statements and blocks define the program structure, and CLI and web-server execution have different inputs and output contexts. In this lesson, focus on echo; then compare it with print. Use the example to predict a result before checking it, and record one case where the behavior may differ.
content.why_it_matters: You will use displaying output when building readable, testable PHP programs. Its practical value is knowing which rule applies, what result to expect, and how to handle failure or unexpected input.

content_blocks.title: A small PHP example for Displaying Output

$normalize = static fn (string $value): string => strtolower(trim($value));
echo $normalize("  PHP  ") . PHP_EOL;

common_mistakes.problem: Copying a pattern without understanding its inputs and output.
common_mistakes.why: Small environment or type differences can change behavior.
common_mistakes.fix: Trace one example by hand, name expected outputs, and consult version-matched official docs.

common_mistakes.problem: Ignoring empty, invalid, or boundary input.
common_mistakes.why: Real data rarely matches only the simplest example.
common_mistakes.fix: Add a deliberate edge-case check before relying on the result.

common_mistakes.problem: Making several changes at once while debugging.
common_mistakes.why: It becomes difficult to identify which change caused the behavior.
common_mistakes.fix: Reduce the issue to one small reproducible case, change one cause, and retest.
